title: The PMP Pass Rate: Why Nobody Actually Knows
dek: PMI does not publish a PMP pass rate, so every percentage you've seen is an estimate or a guess. The famous "61%" isn't a pass rate at all — it's a misquoted passing score PMI retired around 2006, and there is no fixed percentage to hit today.

seo.metaTitle: The PMP Pass Rate: Why Nobody Knows
seo.metaDescription: PMI doesn't publish a PMP pass rate, and the famous 61% is a misquoted old passing score. What's actually knowable, and how to prepare anyway.

body.richText: Search for the PMP pass rate and you'll get confident numbers: 61%, 70%, 45%. They're presented as fact, often with a decimal point for authority. Here's the uncomfortable truth — PMI doesn't publish this figure, so none of those numbers comes from the organization that actually has the data.

The honest answer: nobody outside PMI knows the PMP pass rate. PMI has not published it for roughly two decades. Every percentage in circulation is either an estimate from a training provider's own students, an extrapolation from forum reports, or a number copied from another article that was also guessing.

body.text: The 61% is a misquote — and it matters

body.richText: This is the part almost every page gets wrong, and it's worth being precise, because two different things are being confused:

body.caption: Two different measures that get conflated.
rows: The share of candidates who pass the exam
How well an individual candidate must do to pass

body.richText: Until around 2006, PMI's handbook stated that candidates needed roughly 61% of questions correct — that was a passing score, a requirement for one person. It was never a claim about what proportion of candidates passed. Somewhere along the way it got repeated as a "61% pass rate", and that error has been copied across the internet ever since.
So when you see 61% quoted as a pass rate, you're looking at a two-decade-old number about something else entirely.

body.text: There isn't even a fixed percentage to hit

body.richText: PMI retired the simple percentage threshold and now scores the exam psychometrically — questions carry different weights according to their difficulty. The practical consequence is genuinely counterintuitive: two candidates can answer the same number of questions correctly and get different results, if one answered harder questions than the other.

PMI reports your result by performance band across the exam domains — Above Target, Target, Below Target, Needs Improvement — rather than as a score out of 100. There is no published number to aim at, which is why chasing "61%" on practice exams is aiming at a target that no longer exists.

body.text: What we can honestly say about difficulty

body.richText: Dropping the fake precision doesn't leave us with nothing. Several things about the exam's difficulty are verifiable rather than guessed:

items: Eligibility filters the candidate pool first — you need 36 to 60 months of documented project experience just to apply, so nobody sits this exam cold
It's scenario-based rather than recall-based: most questions ask what you would do, not what a term means
Since July 2026 the exam weights agile and hybrid approaches more heavily than predictive, so preparation built only on traditional methods is now a real risk
PMI publishes an Examination Content Outline, which tells you exactly what's covered — that's a far more useful document than any pass-rate rumour

body.richText: The practical takeaway: stop looking for the pass rate and read the Examination Content Outline instead. It's free, it's official, and it tells you what the exam actually tests — which is the only information that changes your odds.

body.text: Why training companies quote numbers anyway

body.richText: Two reasons, and neither is necessarily dishonest. Some providers publish their own students' pass rates, which are real numbers about a self-selected group of people who paid for a course — not about all candidates. Others simply repeat what other sites say. Either way, a high figure makes a course look effective, so there's little incentive to check.

Be especially sceptical of a "99% pass rate" on a course page. Even where it's accurate, it describes people who paid for training and often sat the exam only when their provider judged them ready — a very different population from everyone attempting the PMP.

body.text: What to do instead of worrying about it

richText: The pass rate is unknowable, so it can't inform your decision. What can: whether you qualify, what it costs, and how long it takes. Check eligibility in our

items.question: What is the PMP exam pass rate?
items.answerRichText: PMI does not publish it, so there is no reliable figure. Estimates in circulation range from around 40% to 70%, but they come from training providers' own students or from forum reports rather than from PMI — and the widely quoted 61% is actually a misremembered passing score retired around 2006.

items.question: What score do you need to pass the PMP?
items.answerRichText: There is no published percentage. PMI scores the exam psychometrically, weighting questions by difficulty, and reports results as performance bands across exam domains rather than as a score out of 100. Aiming for a specific percentage on practice tests is chasing a target that no longer exists.

items.question: Is the PMP exam hard?
answerRichText: It's demanding but not designed to trick you. Questions are scenario-based, and since July 2026 the exam emphasises agile and hybrid approaches, so preparation limited to traditional methods is risky.
